architecture_patterns.name: Botnet infection-to-command lifecycle
architecture_patterns.description: High-level lifecycle for understanding the reported threat: exposed asset, compromise, node enrollment, C2 tasking, malicious activity, detection, and recovery.
steps: Inventory and identify exposed assets.
Validate relevant vendor advisories and exposure.
Observe suspicious process, persistence, and network behavior.
Contain confirmed compromise and preserve evidence.
Restore trusted firmware/software, rotate credentials, patch, and verify.
architecture_patterns.safety_note: Conceptual and defensive; omits executable infection and attack instructions.

architecture_patterns.name: Redis exposure abuse chain
architecture_patterns.description: Source-described chain connecting unauthenticated Redis exposure with unauthorized scheduled execution and defense evasion.
steps: Detect whether Redis is reachable from untrusted networks.
Restrict service binding and network access; require appropriate authentication.
Review audit logs and scheduled-task changes for unauthorized activity.
Contain affected hosts and restore secure configuration.
architecture_patterns.safety_note: Do not reproduce the malicious command sequence; the pattern is expressed as an investigation and prevention workflow.

architecture_patterns.name: IoT device hardening
architecture_patterns.description: A layered baseline for routers, cameras, and embedded systems potentially exposed to Mirai-family malware.
steps: Inventory model, firmware, owner, and exposed management services.
Apply vendor-recommended firmware and security updates.
Replace defaults and restrict management to trusted administrators.
Segment IoT/OT devices and restrict outbound communications.
Monitor and maintain a tested recovery process.

architecture_patterns.name: Behavior-based detection
architecture_patterns.description: Correlate independent host and network signals rather than relying on a single domain or signature.
steps: Collect process, scheduled-task, DNS, firewall, and authentication telemetry.
Look for unexpected cron changes, mining processes, unusual restarts, or suspicious outbound traffic.
Correlate with current vendor advisories and validated indicators.
Document confidence and false-positive considerations before response.

architecture_patterns.name: DDoS defense and service recovery
architecture_patterns.description: Operational response for services targeted by a distributed flood.
steps: Activate incident coordination and establish service impact.
Engage upstream provider or DDoS mitigation service.
Apply tested filtering and rate limits while preserving legitimate traffic.
Monitor effectiveness, restore normal operation, and conduct a post-incident review.

architecture_patterns.name: Compromised-device remediation
architecture_patterns.description: A safe workflow for containing and restoring a suspected compromised network appliance.
steps: Isolate the device from untrusted networks.
Preserve relevant logs and evidence when practical.
Restore known-good vendor firmware or replace unsupported hardware.
Rotate credentials and close exposed management/service paths.
Patch, verify, and monitor before returning the device to service.

Maintain an inventory of embedded devices, firmware versions, owners, and management exposure.
Replace default credentials and use unique administrative credentials.
Restrict management interfaces to trusted administrative networks.
Segment IoT and industrial devices from sensitive corporate systems.
Apply vendor-supported firmware updates and retire unsupported devices where necessary.
Monitor unauthorized cron or scheduled-task changes.
Alert on unexpected attempts to disable SELinux or modify host security controls.
Correlate process, network, DNS, Redis, and authentication logs for stronger detection.
Treat reported C2 domains as time-sensitive indicators; verify provenance and freshness before blocking.
Do not infer the current maliciousness of a domain solely from a historical article listing.
Use layered defenses; a single signature or filtering service is not sufficient by itself.
Restrict outbound traffic where operationally feasible to reduce command-channel and abuse options.
Use least privilege to limit the impact of compromise.
Analyze suspicious samples only in isolated, controlled environments.
Preserve relevant evidence before destructive remediation when safe and practical.
After compromise, restore trusted firmware/software and rotate credentials before reconnecting the device.
Confirm and remediate the initial access path to reduce reinfection risk.
For major DDoS events, coordinate with upstream providers and mitigation services.
Tune rate limits and filtering to protect capacity without unnecessarily blocking legitimate users.

examples.name: Recover a compromised router
examples.scenario: A router shows suspicious process behavior or unauthorized scheduled changes.
steps: Isolate it from untrusted networks while preserving safe administration.
Preserve logs and configuration evidence when feasible.
Restore trusted vendor firmware or replace the device.
Rotate credentials, patch, restrict management, and verify before reconnecting.
examples.expected_outcome: A trusted device state and a reduced chance of reinfection.
